B. Judging
SCOPS concluded that "[y Jou do not claim that the beneficiary meets this criterion, and the record
contains no evidence relevant to this criterion." On appeal, the Petitioner argues that in response to
SCOPS' request for evidence (RFE), it provided evidence that the Beneficiary participated as a peer
reviewer for two journals. The record does reflect that the Petitioner claimed eligibility for this
criterion and identified supporting evidence. Specifically, in the RFE response letter, the Petitioner
stated:
3
In the RFE, the Service noted that the Petitioner did not submit evidence for this
criterion. Please find enclosed, new evidence establishing that [the Beneficiary] has
,=.=:==.c;ated as a peer reviewer for thel I
a renowned ·oumal in the field of chemistry (the #12 ranked journal on
~--------------~ [RFE Exhibit 8]. We therefore submit that
[the Beneficiary] has met his criterion.
However, for the reasons discussed below, the Petitioner's evidence does not demonstrate the
Beneficiary's qualification.
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(4) requires "[e]vidence of the alien's participation on
a panel, or individually, as a judge of the work of others in the same or in an allied field of
specialization to that for which classification is sought." An example of relevant evidence may
include, but is not limited to, peer reviewer for scholarly publications. See generally 2 USCIS Policy
Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
The Petitioner submitted emails from third parties requesting the Beneficiary to conduct manuscript
reviews. Specifically:

participated in the judging of the work of others in the same or allied field of specialization. See

For the reasons discussed above, the Petitioner did not establish the Beneficiary satisfies this criterion.

C. Contributions
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5) requires "[e]vidence of the alien's original
scientific, scholarly, or business-related contributions of major significance in the field." Analysis
under this criterion focuses on whether the beneficiary's original work constitutes major, significant
contributions in the field. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
The Petitioner argues that the Beneficiary "was invited to present her original research at prestigious
international conferences." Evidence that the beneficiary's work was fonded, patented, or published,
while potentially demonstrating the work's originality, will not necessarily establish, on its own, that
the work is of major significance in the field. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at
M.4(C)(2). Although the Petitioner offered evidence of the Beneficiary's presentations at several
conferences, including winning best poster discussed under the awards criterion, the Petitioner did not
contextualize or show the impact of her presentations in the field. The Petitioner did not demonstrate,
for example, that any of her presentations resulted in majorly significant contributions in the field.
While the Petitioner contends that "[t]he fact that the Beneficiary was invited to such prestigious
conferences shows the originality of her work and major significance to the industry," without
supporting documentation showing the impact, influence, or effect in the field in a majorly significant
5
manner, the Petitioner did not establish that simply presenting original work at conferences, even at
prestigious ones, indicates original contributions of major significance in the field.
Likewise, the Petitioner contends that the Beneficiary "and her work have been funded by the U.S.
National Institute of Health and the U.S. National Science Foundation." Although the Petitioner
provided the Beneficiary's co-authored articles indicating funding sources, the Petitioner did not
supplement the record showing how the research or articles impacted, influenced, or affected the field
in a majorly significant fashion. 3 Again, evidence that the beneficiary's work was funded, patented,
or published, while potentially demonstrating the work's originality, will not necessarily establish, on
its own, that the work is of major significance in the field. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual,
supra, at M.4(C)(2).
Regarding the Beneficiary's overall citation record, the Beneficiary provided her Google Scholar
profiles from March 2025 and, in response to SCOPS' RFE, from July 2025.4 Her most recent profile
reflected 193 citations to her co-authored publications, with her three highest-cited articles receiving
69, 56, and 37 citations, respectively. 5 The record, however, does not establish how many of these are
self-citations by her or her coauthors. Nonetheless, this criterion requires a petitioner to establish the
beneficiary's original contributions of major significance in the field. Thus, the burden is on the
petitioner to identify the original contributions and explain how or why they are considered to be of
major significance in the field. Here, the Petitioner did not show the significance of the Beneficiary's
citations to her individual papers or that her papers received citations compared to other articles the
field views as majorly significant. Documentation that published research has been highly cited
relative to other works in that field may be probative of the significance of the beneficiary's
contributions to the field of endeavor. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
Further, the Petitioner provided 2024 data from Clarivate Analytics (InCites Essential Science
Indicators) regarding baseline citation rates and percentiles by year of publication highlighting the
"Chemistry" research field. The Petitioner contends that "[ a ]ccording to a respectable research
analytics company, Clarivate Analytics, [the Beneficiary's] all-time citation count places her among
the top 1% of all cited researcher in the field of chemistry." However, the Petitioner again did not
indicate whether it factored in any self-citations in determining these percentile rankings. Regardless,
the Petitioner did not demonstrate how the Beneficiary's cumulative number of citations represents
contributions of major significance in the field. Moreover, aggregate citation figures tend to reflect
an individual's overall publication record rather than identifying which research or findings, if any,
the field considers to be majorly significant. In addition, the documentation from Clarivate Analytics
states that "[c ]itation frequency is highly skewed, with many infrequently cited papers and relatively
few highly cited papers. Consequently, citation rates should not be interpreted as representing the
central tendency ofthe distribution." Therefore, considering Clarivate Analytics' admission ofhighly
skewed data, the Petitioner did not show the reliability ofthe figures, and therefore, reflects very little,
if any, probative value.
3 The Beneficiary is not listed as the individual responsible for obtaining the funding or research grants; instead, the
Beneficiary is listed as one of several authors who authored the papers in which funding was used to conduct the research.
I
4 Similarly, the Petitioner also provided screenshots from lreflecting reads and citations for nine of the
Beneficiary's publications.
5 The Petitioner's remaining 7 articles received 8 or less as of July 2025.
6
Moreover, citation frequency, which is quantitative in nature, does not reveal the reasons for the
citations, which involve a qualitative analysis. In other words, a high citation number might show that
others in the field have noticed the Beneficiary's work, but it does not confirm that such work or
research has risen to the level of major significance. Regarding a qualitative analysis of the citations,
while they may indicate some degree of interest in her research from her colleagues and peers in the
field, this evidence is not sufficient without supporting material to demonstrate a degree considered to
be majorly significant. Cf, Agrawal v. Miller, No. 4:24CV3143, 2025 WL 2879217, at *20 (D. Neb.
Sept. 12, 2025) (upholding that plaintiff did not provide evidence demonstrating that work has been
widely cited); Bhanu v. Garland, No. CV 22-103, 2023 WL 6119357, at *7-8 (E.D. Pa. Sept. 18, 2023)
(upholding plaintiff did not demonstrate the number of citations received by his published articles
reflect a level of interest in his work from relevant parties to meet this criterion); Gadhave, 2023 WL
6931334, at *5 (f inding the record contained little evidence that contextualized the number ofcitations
the petitioner's work had received); Jafarov v. United States Citizenship & Immigr. Servs., No. 23 CIV.
3372 (PAE), 2024 WL 69056, *7 (S.D.N.Y. Jan. 5, 2024) (finding the absence ofdetail about the actual
impact of the petitioner's work and the limited citations his work had thus far received meant that he
did not satisfy this criterion).
Finally, the Petitioner claims that it "provided ample detailed letters from experts in the field
explaining the nature and signature of the Beneficiary's original contributions." However, the
referenced letters are not sufficiently persuasive. The letters generally highlight the Beneficiary's
work and indicate implementation of the findings into their own work but do not elaborate and
demonstrate how her work is considered to be majorly significant. For example, C-V- indicated that
the Beneficiary's "research, for the first time, is able to detect isonitrile in natural products," and the
Beneficiary "successfully created a protocol to enhance my own research and the broader fields of
synthetic chemistry and pharmaceuticals."6 Although S-N- claimed that the research enhanced "the
broader fields," he did not further explain this claim or detail how the research has impacted or
influenced the wider field rather than limited to S-N-'s own research. Cf, Visinscaia, 4 F. Supp. 3d at
134 (finding the term "major significance in the field" can be reasonably interpreted to mean that there
must be some impact "in the field as a whole"); see also Hristov v. Roark, No. 09-CV-2731, 2011 WL
4711885, at *11 (E.D.N.Y. Sep. 30, 2011); Skokos v. United States Dep't of Homeland Sec., No.
209CV00193RLHPAL, 2010 WL 11538054, at *4 (D. Nev. Jan. 13, 2010), ajf'd sub nom. Skokos v.
US. Dep't ofHomeland Sec., 420 F. App'x 712 (9th Cir. 2011).
Similarly, B-M- stated that "we were able to establish novel technology in a new freshwater
monitoring tool that can detect guanitoxin in freshwater sources," and "[t]he kits have been licensed
I
by the Australian company,! which are offering these kits under the brand
I I'
However, B-M- did not further discuss the kits or address the significance of them
besides being licensed by a company. He did not, for instance, indicate whether the kits are being
widely used or how they have affected the field in a majorly significant way.
Detailed letters from experts in the field explaining the nature and significance of the beneficiary's
contribution may also provide valuable context for evaluating the claimed original contributions of
major significance, particularly when the record includes documentation corroborating the claimed
significance. See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2). Submitted letters should
6 Although we discuss a sample of letters, we have reviewed and considered each in the record.
7
specifically describe the beneficiary's contribution and its significance in the field and should set forth
the basis of the writer's knowledge and expertise. Id. Here, the letters point to the Petitioner's work
but do not demonstrate how the field views it as original contributions of major significance in the
field, such as widespread impact or influence. Cf, Gadhave, 2023 WL 6931334, at *5 (finding
testimonial letters contained mostly general, conclusory statements about the value of the petitioner's
research without explaining in detail specific ways in which his contributions have already been
widely applied or replicated to serve the industry); Jafarov, 2024 WL 69056, at *8 (finding the
petitioner's testimonial evidence spoke largely in generalities and did not evidence the tangible impact
of his work in the field); Noroozi v. Napolitano, 905 F. Supp. 2d 535,544 (S.D.N.Y. 2012) (upholding
reference letters with limited detail on petitioner's satisfaction of regulatory criterion insufficient to
form the basis for required evidence).
For the reasons discussed above, considered both individually and collectively, the Petitioner did not
demonstrate the Beneficiary meets this criterion.
